Why People Follow and Buy: The Psychology That Actually Holds Up

7 min read · Updated November 2026 · Free · Written for Kenya
Share: WhatsApp X Facebook Telegram LinkedIn

The world's most famous shopping study says too much choice kills sales. When researchers pooled 50 experiments on it, the average effect was close to zero.

Marketing is full of 'psychology hacks' copied from old studies. Some are rock solid. Some have failed when scientists tried to repeat them. This lesson shows you which is which.

d = 0.04
Ego depletion (the idea that willpower runs out like a battery) tested in 23 labs with 2,141 people: a result consistent with no effect (Hagger et al., 2016, reported by Discover)

What holds up, what's shaky

IdeaWhat it meansHow to use itHow solid?
Social proofPeople copy what people like them doShow real reviews, customer photos, 'X people from Rongai ordered this week'Strong. Field tests show it, best when the 'others' feel similar
ReciprocityWe feel we owe people who helped us firstGive a genuinely useful tip, price guide or sample before askingWell established (Cialdini's Influence); works only if the gift is real
Familiarity (mere exposure)We tend to like what we see oftenSame face, colours and posting rhythm so people meet you again and againSolid in labs, but repetition can deepen dislike if people already dislike you
Unity'One of us' beats 'like us'Speak to a shared identity: Kisumu mums, campus hustlers, matatu fansNewest of Cialdini's seven (added 2016)
Loss aversionLosses always hurt more than gainsUse carefully; don't build every caption on fearContested: a 2018 review says it depends on context
Choice overloadMore options always mean fewer salesTest it; a clear 'most popular' label often helps more than cutting optionsWeak: meta-analysis average near zero
Ego depletionTired buyers have no willpower leftDon't plan your selling around itFailed a large multi-lab replication
✗ MYTH

Losses hurt twice as much as gains, so scare people into buying ('LAST CHANCE!!').

✓ REALITY

Gal and Rucker's review in the Journal of Consumer Psychology (2018) argues loss aversion has been overgeneralised: when studies separate 'losing' from 'changing', the effect often disappears. What is reliable is inertia: people stick with what they already do. So your real job is making switching to you feel easy and safe, not frightening.

The question behind every purchase: what job is this hired for?

Clayton Christensen's jobs-to-be-done idea says people don't buy products, they 'hire' them to make progress in a specific situation. In his famous example, a fast-food chain found many morning milkshakes were bought by commuters who wanted something to make a long, boring drive less dull. Their real competitors were bananas and bagels, not other milkshakes.

A Nairobi salon isn't only selling braids. For one client the job is 'look sharp for a job interview on Monday'; for another it's 'hair I don't have to think about for six weeks'. Same service, different job, different caption.

💡 What most creators miss

Social proof works best when the 'others' are similar to the viewer. In a hotel study, a card saying most guests reuse towels beat a plain 'save the environment' card (44.1% vs 35.1% reuse), and naming guests who stayed in the same room did even better. 'Students at Kenyatta University love this' will usually beat '10,000 happy customers'.

📋 Job statement + proof caption
JOB STATEMENT (fill for your top 3 customers):
When I'm [SITUATION, e.g. starting a new job next week],
I want to [PROGRESS, e.g. look put-together without spending all Saturday at the salon],
so I can [OUTCOME, e.g. walk in confident].

CAPTION THAT USES IT:
[SITUATION]? This is for you. [WHAT YOU DO] in [TIME / PRICE IN KES].
[REAL PROOF: '14 clients from Kilimani booked this last month' or a customer quote with permission]
DM '[KEYWORD]' and I'll send prices.
✅ Do this today (under 15 minutes)
⚡ Quick check

A friend says: 'Never show more than six products. The jam study proved too much choice kills sales.' What's most accurate?

The 2000 jam study was real, but a 2010 meta-analysis of 50 experiments found an average effect near zero. Choice overload can happen in some conditions, so test your own page instead of trusting the legend.

🧠 Key takeaways
  1. Social proof, reciprocity and familiarity hold up. Make proof specific and from people like your viewer.
  2. Loss aversion is overstated; inertia is real, so make switching to you easy and safe.
  3. Ego depletion failed a big replication and choice overload is weak on average. Don't build on them.
  4. Ask what 'job' a customer hires you for. That job is your caption.
